title: Sellafield pleaded guilty to cyber offences. What that means.
narrative_md:
**The nuclear site holding 140 tonnes of plutonium admitted in court it couldn't keep its own IT systems safe.**

In October 2024, Sellafield Ltd pleaded guilty at Westminster Magistrates' Court to criminal offences under the Nuclear Industries Security Regulations 2003 — the first ever such prosecution of a UK nuclear licensee. The Office for Nuclear Regulation found the Cumbrian site had left IT security failings unaddressed from 2019 to early 2023.

Sellafield is unique. It is not a working power station but the UK's nuclear rubbish bin: 240 tonnes of uranium, 140 tonnes of civil plutonium (the world's largest stockpile), and four 'legacy ponds' containing decades of unprocessed fuel waste. The decommissioning mission runs to 2125 and costs roughly £2.7 billion a year. The Nuclear Decommissioning Authority puts total UK nuclear liability at £140 billion-plus in 2024 prices.

The ONR prosecution narrowly concerned cyber security: insufficient controls over access to sensitive computer systems, failures to implement recommended technical controls, and inadequate assurance reporting to the regulator. The ONR was explicit that no confidential data had been compromised and that the breaches did not cause a safety incident. But the guilty plea matters for what it signals about organisational culture at a site described by the NAO in 2024 as having 'intolerable risks.'

The fine, imposed on 2 October 2024, was £332,500 plus costs — derisory against a £2.7 billion annual budget. The reputational damage was larger. The Guardian's 2023 'Nuclear Leaks' investigation had already alleged much worse — that Sellafield's networks were hacked by groups linked to Russia and China, an allegation the company and ONR denied. The criminal conviction confirmed that the underlying control weaknesses were real, even if the espionage claims remain unproven.

The fiscal implication routes through DESNZ, which funds Sellafield via the NDA. Every extension of the decommissioning timeline — and every remediation programme triggered by regulatory findings — adds to a liability that already dwarfs the annual DESNZ budget. The 2024 Spending Review confirmed the NDA's settlement but with tighter performance reporting; Sellafield's executive chairman resigned in April 2024.

There is a wider reading. The UK's nuclear estate is run by ALBs with budgets larger than some government departments, operating at a technical complexity few ministers or MPs can scrutinise. Accountability tends to arrive either through NAO reports that produce headlines and no consequences, or through extraordinary events like a criminal prosecution. The Sellafield case is the first time the latter mechanism has been used against a nuclear licensee in UK history.

The four legacy ponds remain. So does the plutonium. The IT systems, presumably, are now more robust. The £140 billion bill is not.
